Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verse 7–14:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾ has two interpretations:

One: "I saw a fire." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, and from it the word insan (human being) derives its name, because they are visible (mar'iyyun).

The second: "I sensed a fire." This was said by Qatada. And al-Iyas (perceiving) means sensing from a direction by which one is made to feel comforted (yu'nasu biha).

﴿I will bring you from it a piece of news﴾ has two interpretations:

One: "I will inform you about it with knowledge." This was said by Ibn Shajara.

The second: "a piece of news about the way," because he had lost his way. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand (shihab qabas)﴾. Al-Shihab is a bright shining ray, and from it the star whose light passes across the sky is called shihab. The poet said:

؎ In his hand is a straight, well-shaped spear, in which is a point like the flame of a burning brand (qabas).

Al-Qabas is a piece of fire. From it comes the expression iqtabastu al-nar, meaning I took a piece of it. And iqtabastu minhu 'ilman, if you take knowledge from someone, because you are guided by it just as you are guided by fire.

﴿That perhaps you may warm yourselves (la'allakum tasTalunа)﴾, meaning, so that you may warm yourselves against the cold. Qatada said: and it was winter.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But when he came to it﴾ means he thought it was fire, while it was light. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Musa saw the fire, he stood near it and saw it coming out of the branch of a green tree of intense greenness called al-'Alīq. The fire did not increase except in blazing and greatness, and the tree did not increase except in greenness and beauty. He was amazed by it, drew near, and reached toward it with a bundle of sticks in his hand to take a brand from it. It inclined toward him, so he feared it and drew back from it. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, until he placed its matter as something commanded, while not knowing what its matter was, until: ﴿He was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it."﴾ In ﴿Blessed (bu'ika)﴾ there are three interpretations:

One: it means sanctified (quddisa). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: exalted (tabāraka). This was related by al-Naqqash.

The third: blessing in the fire. This was related by Ibn Shajara, who recited a verse for 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr:

؎ So blessed be among your sons and among theirs, whenever they are mentioned, and we are your ransom.

Regarding "in the fire," there are two views:

One: that it is a fire in which there is light.

The second: that it is light in which there is no fire, and this is the view of the majority.

Regarding ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ there are five sayings:

One: "Blessed is the fire," and ﴿man﴾ is superfluous. In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "Blessed is the fire and whoever is around it." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "Blessed is the light that is in the fire." This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: "Blessed is God who is in the light." This was said by Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: that they are the angels. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: the tree, because the fire blazed within it while it was green and did not burn.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and whoever is around it﴾ there are two interpretations:

One: the angels. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Musa. This was said by Abu Sakhr.

﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ has two interpretations:

One: that Musa said, when he finished hearing the call from the words of God, "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds," seeking help from God and declaring Him free of imperfection. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that this is from the words of God, and its meaning is: "Blessed is whoever glorifies God, Lord of the worlds." This was related by Ibn Shajara.

And this would be part of the speech with which Musa was called.

Regarding that speech there are two views:

(p-196) One: that it is the speech of God, Exalted, from the heaven, at the tree. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Then Musa did not touch a woman after his Lord had spoken to him.

The second: that God created in the tree a speech that came out of it until Musa heard it. This was related by al-Naqqash.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. Wahb said: Musa thought that God had commanded him to abandon it, so he abandoned it.

﴿But when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾ has two interpretations:

One: that the jann is a small serpent, so named because it hides and conceals itself.

The second: that by the jann he meant a devil among the jinn, because they liken everything that frightens them to a devil, as the Exalted said: ﴿Its shoots are as if they were the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65]. The transformation of the staff was into the greatest of serpents, not the smallest, as the Exalted said: ﴿Then behold, it was a clear serpent﴾ [al-A'raf: 107] and [al-Shu'ara: 33]. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas said: The staff had been given to him by one of the angels when he set out for Madyan, and its name was "What-I-Wish" (ma sha'a). Ibn Jubayr said: it was of 'awsaj (thorn wood).

﴿He turned back retreating and did not look back (wa lam yu'aqqib)﴾ has three interpretations:

One: and did not return. This was said by Mujahid. Qutrub said: it is derived from al-'aqib (heel).

The second: and did not wait. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: and did not turn his head. This was said by Qatada.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that it means he remained and did not walk, because in walking one leaves a heel (i.e., a footprint) behind the foot.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. It was said that he meant in the place where revelation is sent to them, otherwise messengers fear God more.

(p-197) ﴿Except one who has done wrong﴾ has two interpretations:

One: that he meant those other than Muslims, because prophets do not commit wrongdoing, and this exception is disjunctive (munqati').

The second: that the exception refers to the messengers.

Upon this there are two views:

One: regarding what they did before prophethood, like Musa's killing of the Copt. But after prophethood they are protected from major and minor sins alike.

The second: after prophethood, they are protected in it even though minor sins may exist in them, except that God showed them kindness by granting them the success of repenting from them. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then I substitute good after evil﴾, meaning repentance after a misdeed.

﴿Indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning Forgiving of their sin and Merciful in accepting their repentance.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verses 20–21:

His saying: ﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ It was said that when Sulayman travelled, the birds would shade him from the sun, and the hoopoe was negligent in its place. Its distance from him became apparent when the sun rose upon him, and the hoopoe was his guide to water. It was also said that the earth was like glass to the hoopoe, so it could see what lay beneath it and would point out the places of water until they arrived. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Whenever they travelled, the hoopoe would dig out for them the nearest water in the earth." Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said: "How does it know the nearest water to the earth, yet not know of the snare until it is seized by its neck?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "Woe to you, O Nafi'! Do you not know that when the decree comes, caution is gone?" Then Sulayman asked about the hoopoe's departure from its place: ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?﴾ That is, has it moved from its place, or has it gone away?

(p-202) ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾. In this there are three aspects:

The first: that he plucked its feathers so that it could not defend itself against anything. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he would make it need its own kind.

The third: that he would place it with its opposites.

﴿Or I will surely slaughter him, or he will bring me a clear authority﴾. In this there are two aspects:

One of them: with a clear proof.

The second: with an evident excuse. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾, that is, with true and genuine information. Regarding ﴿Saba'﴾ there are two views:

The first: It is a city in the land of Yemen called Ma'rib, between it and San'a' is a three-night journey. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Suddi said: God sent to Saba' twelve prophets. And the poet said:

"From Saba', those present at Ma'rib, when they were building, beyond its flood, the dam."

The second: Saba' is a tribe from the tribes of Yemen. Those who held this view differed about their lineage. Some held that it is the name of a woman who was their mother. Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about Saba', and he said: 'He is the son of a man who had ten sons. Six of them were in Yemen and four were in Syria. As for the Yemenis, they are Madhhij, Juhaynah, Kindah, Anmar, al-Azd, and al-Ash'ariyyun. As for the Syrians, they are Lakhm, Judham, 'Amilah, and Ghassan.'" It was also said that he is Saba' ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan.

Al-Mufaddal said: He was named Saba' because he was the first to take captives (sabá).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them﴾. Al-Hasan said: She is Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil, queen of Saba'. Zuhayr ibn Muhammad said: She is Bilqis, daughter of Sharahbil ibn Malik ibn al-Dayyan, and her mother was Fari'ah, a jinn. It was said that she had forty kings as her descendants, the last of whom was Sharahbil.

Qatadah said: Her counselors were three hundred and twelve men, each one of whom was over ten thousand men.

﴿And she has been given of all things﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: Of all things in her land. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: Of all the kinds of worldly goods. This was said by Sufyan.

﴿And she has a great throne﴾. In this there are four sayings:

The first: It is a couch. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: It is a chair (kursi). This was said by Sufyan.

The third: It is a seat of assembly. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: It is kingship. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Regarding His saying ﴿great﴾ there are three meanings:

The first: Massive.

The second: Of fine craftsmanship. This was said by Zuhayr.

The third: Because it was made of gold, its legs were pearls, it was covered with brocade and silk, and it had seven hangings. This was said by Qatadah.

Ibn Ishaq said: Women used to serve her, so there were six hundred women with her for her service.

His saying: ﴿Why do they not prostrate to God, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: It means the hidden things of the heavens and the earth. This was said by Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Jubayr.

The second: The hidden thing of the heavens is rain, and the hidden thing of the earth is plants. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Al-khabʾ (the hidden) in the sense of "that which is concealed," and the verbal noun is used in the place of the adjective.

Regarding the meaning of al-khabʾ in the lexicon there are two views:

The first: It is that which is absent.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verses 27–31:

His saying: ﴿He said: "We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars"﴾, the verse, this is Sulayman's saying to the hoopoe. He said: he was tested and examined in that, and he found him truthful.

﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them﴾. Mujahid said: the hoopoe took the letter in its beak and came to her chamber (bahw), and began to circle around in it. She said: "I have never seen anything better since I saw this bird in my chamber." Then he dropped the letter before her.

Qatadah said: he dropped it upon her chest while she was sleeping. Yazid ibn Ruman said: she was ruling over those who had passed before from her people, and she had been governed, and then she governed until that made her firm.

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: stay near them.

﴿And see what they return⁠—﴾ There is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, its estimated meaning being: "Deliver it to them, then see what they return, then withdraw from them." This was related by Ibn Isa, and al-Farra' said it.

His saying: ﴿She said: "O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me"﴾. Regarding her description of the letter as noble, there are four aspects:

The first: because it was sealed; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: because of the excellence of what is in it; this was said by Qatadah.

The third: because of the nobility of its sender and that he was a king; related by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: because of the hoopoe's being subjected to carrying it.

And it may admit a fifth: because it was thrown down upon her from high, from the direction of the sky.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman﴾, the verse. As for her saying that it is from Sulayman, it is to inform them of the sender of the letter and who he is.

As for her saying: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, it is to express astonishment at this opening which neither she nor her people knew, because the first to open with ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ was Sulayman.

Ibn Buraydah related on the authority of his father, who said: "I was walking with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he said: 'I know a verse that was not revealed to any prophet before me except Sulayman ibn Dawud.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what verse is it?' He said: 'I will teach it to you before I leave the mosque.' He said: then he reached the door and lifted one of his feet, and I said: 'He has forgotten.' Then he turned to me and said: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾."

Asim related from al-Sha'bi who said: "The letters of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were four letters. He used to write: 'In Your name, O Allah.' Then when ﴿In the name of Allah be its sailing and its anchoring﴾ [Hud: 41] was revealed, he wrote: 'In the name of Allah.' Then when ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Isra': 110] was revealed, he wrote: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful.' Then when ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ was revealed, he wrote: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.'"

Asim said: I said to al-Sha'bi: "I have seen a letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ — he said: "That is the third letter."

As for his saying: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission﴾, these are the letters of the prophets, concise and restricted to calling to obedience, without expansion or elaboration.

Regarding ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾ there are three sayings:

The first: do not oppose me; said by Qatadah.

The second: do not be arrogant toward me; said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The third: do not refuse me; said by Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿And come to me in submission﴾ has four interpretations:

The first: submitting; said by al-Kalbi.

The second: monotheists; said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: sincere; said by Zuhayr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verses 36–37:

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿When he came to Sulayman﴾ have two interpretations:

One: "When its gifts came to Sulayman." This is related from Yazid ibn Ruman.

The second: "When its messengers came to Sulayman," because the hoopoe had already gone ahead to Sulayman and informed him of the gift and the messengers, so Sulayman made ready for them.

al-Suddi said: He commanded the devils, and they overlaid the bricks and walls of the city with gold and silver. It was also said that she sent with her messengers a staff which the kings of Himyar had inherited, and she said: "I want him to tell me which end of this is the top." And a cup, and she said: "Let him fill it with water that is neither from the earth nor from the sky." And two pearls (kharazatayn), one of which had a crooked hole, and she said: "Let him thread a string through it." And the other was not drilled, and she said: "Let him drill this one."

﴿He said﴾, Sulayman said to the messengers when they reached him: ﴿Will you provide me with wealth?﴾ Its meaning: "Will you add wealth to me beyond what you see of my riches?"

﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾, that is: what Allah has given me of prophethood and kingship is better than what He has given you of wealth. So he returned the wealth to them, distinguished the boys from the girls, and sent the staff to the ground and said: "Whichever end reached the earth first, that is its root." He commanded the horses to be run until they sweated, and he filled the cup with their sweat and said: "This is neither from the earth nor from the sky." He drilled one of the two pearls and threaded the string through the other. The messengers then testified to what they had witnessed.

It is disputed whether the messengers were men or women, on two views.

As for His words ﴿Return to them﴾, there are two views:

The Prophet of Allah Sulayman (ﷺ) spoke truly, for among his soldiers are humans, jinn and birds, and no one has the power to withstand them.

﴿And we will surely drive them out from it, humbled﴾ — the verse.

It is an announcement to them of what he will do to them, so that whoever is guided among them may be made happy through faith; and this is the practice of every prophet.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on surah 27, verses 38–40:**

His saying, ﴿O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne?﴾ and the verse...

Yazid ibn Ruman related that when her envoys returned with the gifts, she said: "By God, I have known that he is not a king, and we have no power against him." Then she sent to him: "I am coming to you with the kings of my people." She ordered her throne to be placed in seven chambers, one inside another, locked the doors upon it, and set out toward Sulayman with twelve thousand *qayl* (chieftains) from the kings of Yemen. When Sulayman learned of her coming, he said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne?﴾ and the verse. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: ﴿submitting﴾, meaning surrendering and obedient. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that they come to me as ﴿submitting﴾, meaning out of respect for Islam and the religion of truth. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

If it is asked: why did he order her throne to be brought before they came to him in submission?

It is answered that there are five aspects to the reply:

(p-212) The first: that he wished to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he admired her description when the hoopoe described her, and feared that she would become Muslim, and then her wealth would become forbidden to him, so he wanted to take it before it became forbidden to him by her Islam. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: that he wished to outdo her with it, for kings used to outdo one another in kingship and power. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that he wished to test by this her intellect and shrewdness, and whether she would recognize it or deny it. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: that he wished to make this a sign of the truth of his prophethood, because she had left him in her house and secured him in her stronghold, then came to Sulayman and found that he had already preceded her. This is the view of Wahb.

His saying: ﴿A ifrit of the jinn said﴾. The *ifrit* is the strong, powerful rebel. Abu Salih said: "It is as if it were a mountain." In it there are two interpretations:

The first: that he is one who exaggerates in everything, derived from their saying: "So-and-so is an *ifrit* and a *nifriyah*" when he is extreme in affairs. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The second: its root is *al-'Ufr*, which means the strong, and a *ta'* was added to it, so it became *ifrit*. This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place.﴾ In this there are three sayings:

The first: from your assembly; the assembly is called a *maqam* (station) because its occupant remains (*iqamah*) in it, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed the God-fearing will be in a secure station﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:51].

The second: that he meant a known day on which Sulayman used to stand up to preach to them, exhorting, commanding and forbidding them, and that day was near.

The third: that he meant before you set out from your kingdom toward them as a warrior.

﴿And indeed I am strong and trustworthy concerning it.﴾ ''Strong'' means strong enough to carry it. Regarding ''trustworthy'' there are three sayings:

The first: trustworthy regarding what is in it of jewels and pearls. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Ibn Jarir.

The second: trustworthy in that I will not bring you something other than it in its place. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

(p-213) The third: trustworthy regarding the woman's private part. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Yazid ibn Ruman related that the name of the *ifrit* was Kawdi, and Ibn Abi Talhah related that his name was Sakhr, and al-Suddi related that he was Asif ibn al-Saytar ibn Iblis. God knows best the soundness of this.

His saying: ﴿One who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾. In this there are four sayings:

The first: that he was an angel whom God strengthened Sulayman with, and the knowledge of the Scripture is what God wrote for the children of Adam; the angels had known much of it, so God permitted him to inform Sulayman of it and to bring him the throne he had asked for. This is related by Ibn Bahr.

The second saying: that he was one of Sulayman's soldiers from among the jinn and mankind, and the knowledge he had of the Scripture was the book of Sulayman which he had written to Bilqis, and he knew that the wind was subjugated to Sulayman and that the angels were helping him, so he was assured of this before he brought the throne, before his glance returned to him.

The third saying: that it was Sulayman himself who said that to the *ifrit*.

The fourth saying: that it was the statement of someone else from mankind, and in this there are five sayings:

The first: that he was Malikha. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: that he was Ustum. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: that he was Asif ibn Barkhiya, and he was a righteous man (*siddiq*). This is the view of Ibn Ruman.

The fourth: that he was Dhu al-Nur in Egypt. This is the view of Zuhayr.

The fifth: that he was al-Khadir. This is the view of Ibn Lahi'ah.

And ﴿knowledge of the Scripture﴾ is the Greatest Name of God (*ism Allah al-a'zam*), which when called upon by it, He answers.

﴿I will bring it to you﴾, meaning the throne.

﴿Before your glance returns to you.﴾ In this there are six aspects:

The first: before it comes to you from the farthest point you look at. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

The second: before your glance returns to the extent of your sight. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The third: before your glance returns to your assembly. This is the view of Idris.

The fourth: before the time you are awaiting its arrival, from their saying: "I extend my glance toward you," meaning I am waiting for you. This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

(p-214) The fifth: before the glance of your hope returns disappointed, because hope extends the glance and despair shortens it.

The sixth: before your glance diminishes through death; he informed him that he would come to him before his death.

﴿So when he saw it settled beside him﴾, before his glance returned, because the one who had knowledge from the Scripture called upon the Greatest Name of God, and Sulayman's glance returned to it, and there was the throne before him.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: "Sulayman did not know that name, though he had been given what he had been given."

al-Suddi said: "Sulayman was alarmed and said: 'Others are more capable of what is with God than I am,' and then he said, 'Indeed to God we belong and to Him we return.'"

﴿He said: this is of the bounty of my Lord﴾, meaning the throne's arrival to me before my glance returned to me.

﴿To test me: whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ Zuhayr said:

*"Shall I give thanks for the throne, since I was given it so swiftly,*
*or shall I be ungrateful, and not give thanks, since I see one more knowing than me in this world?"*

Zuhayr said: "Then God resolved him to gratitude, and he said: ﴿And whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for himself﴾, because gratitude is the discharge of a right and the solicitation of increase."

﴿And whoever is ungrateful — indeed my Lord is Free of need﴾ from gratitude ﴿Generous﴾ in bestowing favour. This was a miracle for Sulayman, which God brought about through the hand of one of His friends whom He had singled out.

The throne was in Yemen and Sulayman was in al-Sham. It is said that God moved the earth with it until it came to be before him.

His saying, ﴿O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne?﴾ and the verse...

Yazid ibn Ruman related that when her envoys returned with the gifts, she said: "By God, I have known that he is not a king, and we have no power against him." Then she sent to him: "I am coming to you with the kings of my people." She ordered her throne to be placed in seven chambers, one inside another, locked the doors upon it, and set out toward Sulayman with twelve thousand *qayl* (chieftains) from the kings of Yemen. When Sulayman learned of her coming, he said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne?﴾ and the verse. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: ﴿submitting﴾, meaning surrendering and obedient. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that they come to me as ﴿submitting﴾, meaning out of respect for Islam and the religion of truth. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

If it is asked: why did he order her throne to be brought before they came to him in submission?

It is answered that there are five aspects to the reply:

(p-212) The first: that he wished to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he admired her description when the hoopoe described her, and feared that she would become Muslim, and then her wealth would become forbidden to him, so he wanted to take it before it became forbidden to him by her Islam. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: that he wished to outdo her with it, for kings used to outdo one another in kingship and power. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that he wished to test by this her intellect and shrewdness, and whether she would recognize it or deny it. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: that he wished to make this a sign of the truth of his prophethood, because she had left him in her house and secured him in her stronghold, then came to Sulayman and found that he had already preceded her. This is the view of Wahb.

His saying: ﴿A ifrit of the jinn said﴾. The *ifrit* is the strong, powerful rebel. Abu Salih said: "It is as if it were a mountain." In it there are two interpretations:

The first: that he is one who exaggerates in everything, derived from their saying: "So-and-so is an *ifrit* and a *nifriyah*" when he is extreme in affairs. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The second: its root is *al-'Ufr*, which means the strong, and a *ta'* was added to it, so it became *ifrit*. This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place.﴾ In this there are three sayings:

The first: from your assembly; the assembly is called a *maqam* (station) because its occupant remains (*iqamah*) in it, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed the God-fearing will be in a secure station﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:51].

The second: that he meant a known day on which Sulayman used to stand up to preach to them, exhorting, commanding and forbidding them, and that day was near.

The third: that he meant before you set out from your kingdom toward them as a warrior.

﴿And indeed I am strong and trustworthy concerning it.﴾ ''Strong'' means strong enough to carry it. Regarding ''trustworthy'' there are three sayings:

The first: trustworthy regarding what is in it of jewels and pearls. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Ibn Jarir.

The second: trustworthy in that I will not bring you something other than it in its place. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

(p-213) The third: trustworthy regarding the woman's private part. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Yazid ibn Ruman related that the name of the *ifrit* was Kawdi, and Ibn Abi Talhah related that his name was Sakhr, and al-Suddi related that he was Asif ibn al-Saytar ibn Iblis. God knows best the soundness of this.

His saying: ﴿One who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾. In this there are four sayings:

The first: that he was an angel whom God strengthened Sulayman with, and the knowledge of the Scripture is what God wrote for the children of Adam; the angels had known much of it, so God permitted him to inform Sulayman of it and to bring him the throne he had asked for. This is related by Ibn Bahr.

The second saying: that he was one of Sulayman's soldiers from among the jinn and mankind, and the knowledge he had of the Scripture was the book of Sulayman which he had written to Bilqis, and he knew that the wind was subjugated to Sulayman and that the angels were helping him, so he was assured of this before he brought the throne, before his glance returned to him.

The third saying: that it was Sulayman himself who said that to the *ifrit*.

The fourth saying: that it was the statement of someone else from mankind, and in this there are five sayings:

The first: that he was Malikha. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: that he was Ustum. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: that he was Asif ibn Barkhiya, and he was a righteous man (*siddiq*). This is the view of Ibn Ruman.

The fourth: that he was Dhu al-Nur in Egypt. This is the view of Zuhayr.

The fifth: that he was al-Khadir. This is the view of Ibn Lahi'ah.

And ﴿knowledge of the Scripture﴾ is the Greatest Name of God (*ism Allah al-a'zam*), which when called upon by it, He answers.

﴿I will bring it to you﴾, meaning the throne.

﴿Before your glance returns to you.﴾ In this there are six aspects:

The first: before it comes to you from the farthest point you look at. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

The second: before your glance returns to the extent of your sight. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The third: before your glance returns to your assembly. This is the view of Idris.

The fourth: before the time you are awaiting its arrival, from their saying: "I extend my glance toward you," meaning I am waiting for you. This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

(p-214) The fifth: before the glance of your hope returns disappointed, because hope extends the glance and despair shortens it.

The sixth: before your glance diminishes through death; he informed him that he would come to him before his death.

﴿So when he saw it settled beside him﴾, before his glance returned, because the one who had knowledge from the Scripture called upon the Greatest Name of God, and Sulayman's glance returned to it, and there was the throne before him.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: "Sulayman did not know that name, though he had been given what he had been given."

al-Suddi said: "Sulayman was alarmed and said: 'Others are more capable of what is with God than I am,' and then he said, 'Indeed to God we belong and to Him we return.'"

﴿He said: this is of the bounty of my Lord﴾, meaning the throne's arrival to me before my glance returned to me.

﴿To test me: whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ Zuhayr said:

*"Shall I give thanks for the throne, since I was given it so swiftly,*
*or shall I be ungrateful, and not give thanks, since I see one more knowing than me in this world?"*

Zuhayr said: "Then God resolved him to gratitude, and he said: ﴿And whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for himself﴾, because gratitude is the discharge of a right and the solicitation of increase."

﴿And whoever is ungrateful — indeed my Lord is Free of need﴾ from gratitude ﴿Generous﴾ in bestowing favour. This was a miracle for Sulayman, which God brought about through the hand of one of His friends whom He had singled out.

The throne was in Yemen and Sulayman was in al-Sham. It is said that God moved the earth with it until it came to be before him.

His saying: ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her."﴾ That is, change it. There are five aspects to what changing it involved:

First: he removed from it its settings, its fittings, and its jewels. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-215) Second: he changed what was red into green and what was green into red. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: he altered it by adding to it and subtracting from it. This was said by ʿIkrimah.

Fourth: he turned its upper part to its lower part and its front to its back. This was said by Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Fifth: he altered it by making in it the image of a fish. This was said by Abu Ṣāliḥ.

﴿We shall see whether she is guided or is among those who are not guided.﴾ In this there are two aspects:

One: "Will she be guided to the truth by her intellect, or will she be among those who do not use their intellect?" This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Rūmān.

Second: "Will she be guided to recognizing the throne by her acuteness, or will she be among those who do not recognize it?" This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it."﴾ She neither affirmed it nor denied it. The scholars differed about the reason for her saying that, in three opinions:

One: because she had left it behind her, and then found it in front of her. Her recognition of it prevented her from denying it, and her having left it behind her prevented her from affirming it. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatādah.

Second: because she found in it what she recognized, so she did not deny it, and she found in it what had been changed and altered, so she did not affirm it. This was said by al-Suddī.

Third: they confused her when they said, "Is your throne like this?" so she confused them in return, saying, "It is as if it were it." Had they said to her, "This is your throne," she would have said, "Yes." This was said by Muqātil.

﴿And we were given knowledge before her.﴾ This is a statement of Sulaymān, and it has been said that it is from the speech of his people. In its interpretation there are three opinions:

One: the knowledge of God and His oneness. This was said by Zuhayr.

Second: prophethood. This was said by Yaḥyā ibn Salām.

Third: that is, "We knew that the throne was hers before we asked her." This was said by Ibn Shajara.

﴿And we were Muslims.﴾ In this there are two aspects:

One: obedient to God through submission to Him.

(p-216) Second: sincere to God in His oneness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what she used to worship besides God barred her.﴾ In this there are four aspects:

One: the worship of the sun barred her from worshipping God.

Second: her disbelief in God's decree barred her from being guided to the truth.

Third: Sulaymān barred her from what she used to worship in her disbelief.

Fourth: God Exalted barred her, by guiding her to faith, from disbelief.

His saying: ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace."﴾ In this there are three opinions:

One: it is a pool built of glass. This was said by Mujāhid.

Second: it is the courtyard of the house. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā. It is said ṣarḥat al-dār, sāḥat al-dār, bāḥat al-dār, and qāʿat al-dār, all with the same meaning. Zuhayr said: it is derived from taṣrīḥ (clarity), and from it comes ṣarraḥa bi-l-amr, meaning he made the matter manifest.

Third: that it is a palace (qaṣr). This was said by Ibn Shajara, who cited the verse of al-Hudhalī:

"Upon roads like the necks of gazelles, you think their markers are palaces (ṣurūḥ)."

﴿When she saw it, she thought it was a deep water.﴾ That is, water, because Sulaymān had ordered the jinn to build it of glass over water. They built it and placed around it the likenesses of fish. He ordered her to enter because she had been described to him, and he wished to see her.

Mujāhid said: she was hairy (halbāʾ, meaning long-haired), her shin was like the hoof of a donkey, and her mother was a jinniyya.

Mixing is impossible given such a difference, and procreation is impossible given such divergence. But since it has been said, I have mentioned it as a report.

Fourth: he turned its upper part to its lower part and its front to its back. This was said by Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

al-Ḥasan said: the jinn feared that Sulaymān would marry her, and that through her he would learn things that the jinn had been concealing from him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verses 45–47:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then behold, they became two parties disputing﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

One: a disbeliever and a believer. This is said by Mujahid.

The second: one who affirms and one who denies. This is said by Qatadah.

About what did they dispute? There are two opinions concerning it:

One: that each group says, "We are upon the truth, not you."

The second: they disagreed over whether they knew that Salih was a messenger from his Lord. This is said by Mujahid.

His saying: ﴿He said: "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good?"﴾ There are two opinions concerning it:

One: [it means] hastening punishment before mercy. This is said by Mujahid, based on their saying: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful.﴾

The second: [it means] hastening affliction before well-being. This is said by al-Suddi.

﴿Perhaps you will be shown mercy﴾: there are two interpretations concerning it:

One: [mercy] by sufficiency.

The second: [mercy] by answered supplication.

His saying: ﴿They said: "We consider you and those with you a bad omen."﴾ That is, "We regard you and those with you as ill-omened," derived from tiyarah (omen-taking, the belief that events are foretold by birds or signs). Concerning their taking omen from him, there are two interpretations:

One: because of the division of their word (their unity being broken). This is said by Ibn Shajarah.

The second: because of the evil that befell them. This is said by Qatadah.

﴿He said: "Your omen is with Allah"﴾: there are two interpretations concerning it:

One: your calamities are with Allah. This is said by Ibn Abbas, because they descend upon you swiftly like a bird.

The second: your deeds are with Allah. This is said by Qatadah, because they ascend to Him like a bird.

﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾: there are two interpretations concerning it:

One: you are tested through obedience to Allah and disobedience to Him. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: you are turned away from your religion which Allah has commanded you, which is Islam. This is said by al-Hasan.

**The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on verses 48–53 of Surah al-Naml (27)**

His words: ﴿And there were in the city nine men of a group﴾. The *rahṭ* (a group of men, usually three to ten, with no singular form) are meant here as men from Thamud, the people of Salih, and they are the ones who hamstrung the she-camel. Ibn 'Abbas named them and said: they were Za'ji, Za'im, Harami, Dar, Sawab, Rabab, Misṭa', and Qidar. They lived in the land of al-Hijr, which is the land of Syria, and they were wicked men from the nobles of their people.

﴿Who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾. On this there are five aspects:

The first: they spread corruption by disbelief and did not reform by faith.

The second: they spread corruption by evil and did not reform by good.

(p-220) The third: they spread corruption by sins and did not reform by obedience.

The fourth: they spread corruption by breaking the dirhams and dinars, and did not reform by leaving them whole (*ṣiḥāḥ*). This was said by Ibn al-Musayyab, and it was said by 'Ata'.

The fifth: they used to pursue the private faults of women and did not conceal them.

His words: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by God"﴾, that is, bind yourselves by oath to God.

﴿"That we will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾, that is, that we will kill him and his family at night. *Bayat* (night attack) is killing by night.

﴿"Then we will surely say to his guardian"﴾, that is, to the group of Salih.

﴿"We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾, that is, his killing and the killing of his family, and we did not know of it.

﴿"And indeed, we are truthful"﴾ in our denial of his killing.

﴿And they plotted a plot﴾, which is what they intended of killing Salih.

﴿And We plotted a plot﴾, which is that God struck them with a rock and destroyed them.

﴿While they did not perceive﴾, that is, they did not know of Our plot, though We knew of their plot.

Regarding their plot and God's plot against them, there are two views:

The first: this was said by al-Kalbi. "While they did not perceive" refers to the angels whom God sent down to Salih to protect him from his people when they entered upon him to kill him. Each of them was struck by a stone until they were all killed, and Salih was safe from their plot.

The second: this was said by al-Dahhak. They plotted by showing that they were going on a journey, then they went out and hid in a cave to return at night and kill him. God then cast a rock over the mouth of the cave until it sealed it, and this was God's plot against them.

His words: ﴿And there were in the city nine men of a group﴾. Ibn 'Abbas named them and said: they were Za'ji, Za'im, Harami, Dar, Sawab, Rabab, Misṭa', and Qidar. ﴿Who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾. On this there are five aspects:

The first: they spread corruption by disbelief and did not reform by faith.

The second: they spread corruption by evil and did not reform by good.

The fourth: they spread corruption by breaking the dirhams and dinars, and did not reform by leaving them whole (*ṣiḥāḥ*). This was said by Ibn al-Musayyab, and it was said by 'Ata'.

"His saying: ﴿Is He who made the earth a stable resting place﴾, meaning He made it a place of settlement.

The first: the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the sea of Persia and the sea of the Romans. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: the sea of al-Sham and the sea of Iraq. This was said by al-Suddi.

His saying: ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ He specified the response to the distressed one for two reasons:

The first: because his desire is stronger and his supplication more humble.

﴿And removes the evil﴾ may have two meanings:

The first: that it is removed from the distressed one through responding to him.

The second: that it is removed from the one who has undertaken it, so that it does not befall him.

Regarding ﴿the evil﴾ there are two views:

The first: harm.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verse 65–70:

His saying: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has fallen short concerning the Hereafter﴾. Concerning the description of their knowledge in this way, there are two opinions.

The first: that it is a description of blame. According to this, there are four interpretations of its meaning:

The first: it was hidden from them (ghába ʿalayhim), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: their knowledge was not attained (lam yudrak ʿilmuhum), said by Ibn Muhaysin.

The third: their knowledge perished (idmihall ʿilmuhum), said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: their knowledge went astray (ḍalla ʿilmuhum), which is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

This is the interpretation of those who claim that it is a description of blame.

The second opinion: that it is a description of praise for their knowledge, even though they are blameworthy. According to this, there are three interpretations of its meaning:

The first: their knowledge was attained (udrika ʿilmuhum), said by Mujahid.

The second: their knowledge was gathered together (ijtamaʿa ʿilmuhum), said by al-Suddi.

The third: their knowledge followed one another (talāḥaqa ʿilmuhum), said by Ibn Shajarah.

﴿In doubt about it﴾, meaning about the Hereafter. Whoever takes what precedes as a description of blame for their knowledge holds that the deficiency of their knowledge in the world is what led them to doubt about the Hereafter. Whoever takes that as a description of praise for their knowledge holds that the perfection of their knowledge concerns the Hereafter, and that this does not prevent them from being in doubt about the Hereafter in the world.(p-225)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verses 71–81:

His saying: ﴿radifa lakum﴾ (rarely used; from radifa, "to follow closely" or "to draw near") has three interpretations:

First: its meaning is "it drew near to you and came close to you." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn ʿIsa.

Second: "it hastened for you." This was said by Mujahid.

Third: "it followed you." This was said by Ibn Shajara. From this comes ridf (the rear seat) of a woman, because it follows her from behind. Abu Dhuʾayb said:

؎ ʿAda al-sawadu bayadan fi mafariqihi / la marhaban bi-bayad al-shayb idh radifa
(The blackness returned as whiteness upon his temples; / no welcome to the whiteness of grey hair when it came following.)

In His saying the Exalted: ﴿some of what you are hastening﴾ there are two interpretations:

First: the Day of Badr.

Second: the punishment of the grave.

His saying: ﴿And there is no hidden thing﴾ (the verse).

In it there are three interpretations:

First: the hidden thing is the Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: what is hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Third: all that Allah has concealed from His creation and kept hidden from them. This is related by Ibn Shajara.

Regarding ﴿a clear Book﴾ there are two views:

First: the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

(p-226)
Second: the decree that is determined (al-qada' al-mahtum).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verse 82:

His saying ﴿And when the word has come to pass against them﴾ has four interpretations:

First: the wrath has become due against them. This is related from Qatadah.

Second: when the word has become due against them that they will not believe. This is related from Mujahid.

Third: when they are not commanded to do what is right and forbidden from what is wrong, the displeasure becomes due against them. This is related from Ibn Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Fourth: when the punishment descends. This is related by al-Kalbi.

﴿We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth that will speak to them﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One of them: what Muhammad ibn Ka'b related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he was asked about the creature and said: "By Allah, it has a tail, and it has a beard." In this statement there is an indication that it is from mankind, though he did not state it explicitly.

The second, which is the view of the majority, is that it is a creature among the creatures of the earth. Those who held this differed about its description in three sayings:

First: that it is a creature with down and feathers, having four legs. This is related from Ibn Abbas.

Second: that it is a creature with fur that reaches up towards the sky. This is related from al-Sha'bi.

The third saying: that its head is the head of an ox, its eye is the eye of a pig, its ear is the ear of an elephant, its horn is the horn of a stag, its neck is the neck of an ostrich, its chest is the chest of a lion, its colour is the colour of a leopard, its flank is the flank of a cat, its tail is the tail of a ram, and its legs are the legs of a camel; between each two joints there are twelve cubits. Along with it come the staff of Musa and the seal of Sulayman. It strikes the face of the believer with the staff of Musa, making a white mark, and strikes the face of the disbeliever with the seal of Sulayman, so his face turns black. This is related from Ibn al-Zubayr.

(p-227) Concerning His saying ﴿from the earth﴾ there are four sayings:

First: that it will emerge from some of the valleys of Tihamah. This is related from Ibn Abbas.

Second: from a rock in the valley of Ajyad. This is related from Ibn Umar.

Third: from al-Safa. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud.

Fourth: from the Sea of Sodom. This is related from Ibn Munabbih.

Concerning ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ there are two readings:

The irregular (shadhdhah) one of them: (tasimuhum), with a fatha on the ta'. Concerning its interpretation there are two views:

One of them: it marks them on their faces, with whiteness on the face of the believer and blackness on the face of the disbeliever, until people call out to one another in their markets: "O believer! O disbeliever!" Abu Umamah related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The creature will emerge and mark people on their snouts."

The second: its meaning is that it wounds them. This applies specifically to the disbeliever and the hypocrite, and its wounding is the manifestation of their disbelief and hypocrisy. From this comes the "wounding" of witnesses by declaring them corrupt (tafsiq). This is likely the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second reading, which is the one held by the majority, is ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the lam, from kalam (speech). Qatadah related that in some readings it is: ﴿tunabbi'uhum﴾ (it informs them). Yahya ibn Salam related that in some readings it is: (tuhaddithuhum) (it tells them).

Concerning its speech on this interpretation there are two views:

One of them: that its speech is the manifestation of the signs from it, without utterance or words.

The second view: that it is speech that is spoken.

(p-228) On this view, concerning what it speaks there are two views:

One of them: that it tells them that this one is a believer and this one is a disbeliever.

The second: it tells them what Allah said: ﴿that people were not certain of Our signs﴾. This is said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ata'.

Ibn al-Baylamani related from Ibn Umar that the creature will emerge on the night of Jam', which is the night of sacrifice, while the people are travelling to Mina.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verse 83–86:

His saying: ﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a company of those who denied Our signs﴾. They are its disbelievers who denied.

In His saying ﴿Our signs﴾ there are two opinions:

One of them: Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: all the Messengers. This is the saying of the majority.

﴿Then they will be driven in ranks (yuza'un)﴾. Concerning it there are four opinions:

The first: they will be gathered. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

The second: they will be pushed back. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: they will be driven on. This was said by Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi, and from it is the verse of al-Shammakh:

"How often we were driven (wuzzi'na) from a host of a mighty, armoured army, and how often we bestowed gifts upon a chief of noble lineage."

The fourth: the first of them will be held back until the last of them catches up, as said by Qatada.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 27, verses 87–90:

﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection from the graves. On this there are three opinions:

The first: *al-Ṣūr* is the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), and blowing into it means the restoration of the spirits to them.

The second: it is an object blown into, like a horn, from which emerges a sound by which the dead will be brought to life.

The third: it is a parable (*mathal*) that God struck for the revival of the dead at one time, with their emerging at that moment like the emergence of an army when they are warned by the blowing of a horn, so that they all come out together at one time.

﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom God wills﴾. On this terror here there are two opinions:

The first: it is the responding and hastening toward the call, from your saying "fazi'tu ilayhi min kadha" (I went to him in fear of such-and-such) when you hasten to his call for your aid. The poet said:

"Whenever a crier in distress came to us, his cry was like the rapid beating of the hooves."

On this view, ﴿except whom God wills﴾ is an exception for them from responding and hastening to the Fire.

As to those who are meant, there are two possibilities:

The first: the angels who were delayed from this blast.

The second: the beasts, which will become dust if they are restored.

The second opinion: the terror here is the familiar terror of fear and dread, because they will be driven from their graves and so will be terrified and afraid. This is the more likely of the two opinions. On this view, His saying ﴿except whom God wills﴾ is an exception for them from fear and terror.

Concerning them there are two opinions:

The first: they are the angels whom God makes firm in their hearts. This was said by Ibn ʿĪsā.

The second: they are the martyrs.

Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they are the martyrs. Were it not for this text, the prophets would have a better claim to it, for they do not fall short of the ranks of the martyrs, although this text does point to them.

It is said that Israfil is the one who blows into the Trumpet.

﴿And all will come to Him humbled﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: *rāghimīn* (humiliated), said by al-Suddi.

The second: *ṣāghirīn* (abased), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah. The meaning of His saying ﴿And all will come to Him humbled﴾ is those who were terrified and those excepted from the terror by His saying ﴿except whom God wills﴾. This will be at the second blast, while the terror is at the first blast. Al-Hasan narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Between the two blasts is forty years."

His saying ﴿And you will see the mountains, thinking them fixed﴾, that is, standing still.

﴿Yet they will pass away like the passing of clouds﴾, that is, their motion will not be seen because of the distance of their extremities, just as the motion of clouds is not seen when they spread out because of the distance of their extremities. This is a parable. Concerning what it is a parable for, there are three opinions:

The first: it is a parable God struck for the world. The onlooker thinks it is standing still like the mountains, while it is taking its share of passing away like the clouds. This was said by Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah.

The second: it is a parable God struck for faith, which you think is firmly fixed in the heart while its deeds ascend to heaven.

The third: it is a parable for the soul at the departure of the spirit, when the spirit travels to *al-Quds* (the sacred realm).

(p-231) ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾, that is, the work of God who perfected everything.

Concerning this there are four aspects:

The first: He made everything firm, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: He counted everything, said by Mujahid.

The third: He made everything good, said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: He made everything secure. There is disagreement over the word: al-Dahhak said it is a Syriac word. Others said it is Arabic, derived from *itqān al-shay'* (the perfecting of a thing) when it is made firm and secured, and its root is from *al-taqn*, which is what is heavy of the clay in a basin.

His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed﴾. On this there are two opinions:

The first: it is the performance of all the obligatory duties.

The second: it is better than them, because by one good deed he is given ten. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: "then he will have better than it" refers to the reward that returns to him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

﴿And they will be secure from terror that Day﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: they are secure from the terror of the Day of Resurrection in Paradise.

The second: they are secure from the terror of death in this world, in the Hereafter.

﴿And whoever brings an evil deed﴾: it is polytheism, according to the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Hurayrah.

The first: He made everything firm, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: He counted everything, said by Mujahid.

The third: He made everything good, said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: He made everything secure. There is disagreement over the word: al-Dahhak said it is a Syriac word. Others said it is Arabic, derived from *itqān al-shay'* (the perfecting of a thing) when it is made firm and secured, and its root is from *al-taqn*, which is what is heavy of the clay in a basin.

His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed﴾. On this there are two opinions:

The first: it is the performance of all the obligatory duties.

The second: it is better than them, because by one good deed he is given ten. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: "then he will have better than it" refers to the reward that returns to him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

﴿And they will be secure from terror that Day﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: they are secure from the terror of the Day of Resurrection in Paradise.

The second: they are secure from the terror of death in this world, in the Hereafter.

﴿And whoever brings an evil deed﴾: it is polytheism, according to the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Hurayrah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 27, verses 87–90:

﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection from the graves. On this there are three opinions:

The first: *al-Ṣūr* is the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), and blowing into it means the restoration of the spirits to them.

The second: it is an object blown into, like a horn, from which emerges a sound by which the dead will be brought to life.

The third: it is a parable (*mathal*) that God struck for the revival of the dead at one time, with their emerging at that moment like the emergence of an army when they are warned by the blowing of a horn, so that they all come out together at one time.

﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom God wills﴾. On this terror here there are two opinions:

The first: it is the responding and hastening toward the call, from your saying "fazi'tu ilayhi min kadha" (I went to him in fear of such-and-such) when you hasten to his call for your aid. The poet said:

"Whenever a crier in distress came to us, his cry was like the rapid beating of the hooves."

On this view, ﴿except whom God wills﴾ is an exception for them from responding and hastening to the Fire.

As to those who are meant, there are two possibilities:

The first: the angels who were delayed from this blast.

The second: the beasts, which will become dust if they are restored.

The second opinion: the terror here is the familiar terror of fear and dread, because they will be driven from their graves and so will be terrified and afraid. This is the more likely of the two opinions. On this view, His saying ﴿except whom God wills﴾ is an exception for them from fear and terror.

Concerning them there are two opinions:

The first: they are the angels whom God makes firm in their hearts. This was said by Ibn ʿĪsā.

The second: they are the martyrs.

Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they are the martyrs. Were it not for this text, the prophets would have a better claim to it, for they do not fall short of the ranks of the martyrs, although this text does point to them.

It is said that Israfil is the one who blows into the Trumpet.

﴿And all will come to Him humbled﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: *rāghimīn* (humiliated), said by al-Suddi.

The second: *ṣāghirīn* (abased), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah. The meaning of His saying ﴿And all will come to Him humbled﴾ is those who were terrified and those excepted from the terror by His saying ﴿except whom God wills﴾. This will be at the second blast, while the terror is at the first blast. Al-Hasan narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Between the two blasts is forty years."

His saying ﴿And you will see the mountains, thinking them fixed﴾, that is, standing still.

﴿Yet they will pass away like the passing of clouds﴾, that is, their motion will not be seen because of the distance of their extremities, just as the motion of clouds is not seen when they spread out because of the distance of their extremities. This is a parable. Concerning what it is a parable for, there are three opinions:

The first: it is a parable God struck for the world. The onlooker thinks it is standing still like the mountains, while it is taking its share of passing away like the clouds. This was said by Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah.

The second: it is a parable God struck for faith, which you think is firmly fixed in the heart while its deeds ascend to heaven.

The third: it is a parable for the soul at the departure of the spirit, when the spirit travels to *al-Quds* (the sacred realm).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 27, verses 91–93:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: it is Makkah. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is Mina. This is the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah. Its being made sacred (tahrim) means honouring its sanctity and refraining from hunting its game and cutting its trees.

(p-232) ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾, meaning He owns everything, of what He has made lawful and what He has made unlawful, so He makes lawful from it whatever He wills and makes unlawful from it whatever He wills, because the owner has the right to do whatever he wishes with his property.

His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognise them﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: He will show you them in the Hereafter, and you will recognise them as He described them in this world. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: He will show you in this world the signs that you see in the heavens and the earth, and you will recognise them as true. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾, of good or evil, so He will certainly recompense for it. And God knows best.
